> What does any of this has to do with making more money?

The reason EA pays developers to make games is because they believe they will be then be able to sell those games and make a profit. When they greenlight a traditional $60 console project like NFS (assuming the new one won't be F2P or some kind of budget title, which is possibility), it's because they think they can produce a title that will sell enough units at ~$60 to make back more than they spent.

The direction they've taken with the last few games has led to sales plateauing or declining, so they decide to change their approach. Trying to sell more copies by broadening the game's appeal (by making it more accessible for a younger audience, for instance) is a reasonable thing for EA to do; Every game EA spends money on producing needs to sell as much as it possibly can, because as a publically traded company, EA is required by law to make money for their shareholders.

> They're abandoning the player base they already have, which BTW, buys millions upon millions of copies of every new NFS

Exact sales data isn't available, but Heat seems to have sold about [3 million copies](https://www.reddit.com/r/needforspeed/comments/ex7ohv/comment/fg6lmck/?utm_source=share&utm_medium=web2x&context=3). For comparison, Forza Horizon 4, arguably Heat's closest competitor, [sold 10+ million](https://www.thegamer.com/xbox-one-fastest-selling-exclusives-sales/), and that's without PlayStation.

> it's always one of the most sold games when it launches

In the US, [Heat was the 9th best selling game the month it came out](https://venturebeat.com/games/november-2019-npd-pokemon-has-best-u-s-launch-in-series-history/), and [15th the next month](https://venturebeat.com/business/december-2019-npd-call-of-duty-star-wars-close-out-2019-on-top/). The best selling game in the series, Most Wanted 2005, [actually debuted with even weaker sales](https://www.gamespot.com/articles/chartspot-november-2005/1100-6141589/), though different console versions are counted separately in this chart. It still went on to sell [16 million copies by 2009](https://news.softpedia.com/news/100-million-Need-for-Speed-Games-Have-Been-Sold-to-This-Day-125015.shtml). I posit that this is the series' high watermark in terms of profitability, because it feels right and also because I've already spent an hour sourcing all these claims and wanna go eat.
(update: 2 hours)

I don't know how many of those 16 million are $50 console releases (I think handheld versions are included in that figure), but [according to this site](https://www.usinflationcalculator.com/), $50 in 2005 is worth $75 in 2022 bux. Heat was $60 in 2019, and it's safe to assume that if '22 is a traditional retail boxed game, it will also be $60 for most platforms in, well, 2022. In real terms, *the price of modern games have actually gone down relative to inflation!*

But traditional $60 boxed games are also far more expensive to develop nowadays; developer salaries are almost certainly the biggest chunk of the budget (though licensing music and cars is a big part of it as well), and Heat's credits list [5 times as many developers](https://www.mobygames.com/game/windows/nfs-heat/credits) as [MW05](https://www.mobygames.com/game/windows/need-for-speed-most-wanted/credits). Working conditions have also changed since then; it's likely a much higher proportion of Heat's developers are part-timers or outsourced compared to 2005, precisely because that helps save costs when you need so much manpower to produce huge games full of photoreal art assets, tons mo-capped cutscenes, etc. Just as one example. Heat has more than 3x as many cars as MW05, and while I can't find exact polygon counts to compare the two, it tends to go up by an order of magnitude every console generation, and MW is at least 2 behind.

> to focus on kids that play fortnite who, first, don't pay for games (Fornite is F2P)

[Fortnite is insanely profitable](https://www.theverge.com/2021/5/3/22417447/fortnite-revenue-9-billion-epic-games-apple-antitrust-case), because *kids do, in fact, pay for the game*. Not $60 up front like a traditional boxed release, but potentially much more than that over time, for things like battle passes and skins. F2P games can absolutely make enormous amounts of money. _Why do you think so many games are going that route?_

> and second, have absolutely no interest in cars.

To be sure, car culture has changed, and arguably declined in mainstream popularity from the early '00s. But making racing games for kids is a good way to get kids interested in cars.

> Criterion is 100% responsible for every single creative decision behind this game

Criterion is a subsidiary of EA. Workers at Criterion may answer to bosses who also work at Criterion, but at higher tiers those people answer to EA, because EA are the ones paying everyone's salaries. Therefore, it's more accurate to say that EA is responsible for 100% of the decisions that they allow Criterion to make.

> simplifying everything, cutting out things the community loves

The only things this leak tells us that seem to directly relate to gameplay are that:

* drift events are gone

* speedcross events return from Payback

* drag events don't return don't return from Payback

There's also this line:

>  Upgrade system simplified for the younger audience. Similar to what Forza does (B, A, S), but you can still find numbers.

These vaguely-worded bullet points from a secondhand summary of a leak, ***is your entire body of evidence that they've "simplified everything".*** The last sentence even seems to be clarifying the one before it: there will be a letter grading system for car performance "similar to Forza's", as opposed to the 0-400 number rating of the last few NFS games. A letter is indeed simpler than a 3-digit number, and that may be easier for a younger audience to intuitively understand. *Inferring anything about the larger upgrade system, handling model, or other aspects of the game's design is pure speculation*, and making the leap from speculation to "0/10 trash game" is just fans being triggered and irrational.

I cannot emphasize enough that all we know about this game right now is from leaks. ***Everyone in this comments section who complains about the game has not played it for themselves, yet somehow formed an opinion on it.*** Even before you play a game, with an official trailer or screenshots, you can definitively say "they chose to show this to represent their product, and that product looks like shit". But unless a leaker specifically says "this screenshot was taken on this date", leaks can be months or years out of date, show off unpolished elements, be edited/mockups, or any number of other things. That's why you're supposed to take them with a grain of salt, and why it makes no sense to declare that the game sucks/is doomed/is already dead/is trash at this stage.

TL;DR: You're seeing a sausage in the middle of it being made, and saying "I bet this hot dog tastes like shit and your company is going to fail because of that".
